provenance.other: “one another's burdens” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 6:2, and “bear ye one another” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The second half of the clause is a second singleton: “burden is light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:30. The Book of Mormon reproduces Paul's imperative with the pronoun dropped to fit the construction — 'are willing to bear one another's burdens' — and no other word changed.
provenance.significance: Galatians 6:2 does not stop at the imperative: bearing one another's burdens is how one 'fulfil[s] the law of Christ', and that is what Alma is at this moment constituting — a covenant community defined by a law, in a book whose next hundred pages will argue about the law of Moses. The Matthew half supplies the reason the burdens become bearable: 'my yoke is easy, and my burden is light' is Christ's, and Alma's 'that they may be light' transfers the lightness from the yoke of Christ to the shared load of the congregation. Between them the two singletons make the baptismal covenant a piece of Pauline ecclesiology with a synoptic promise attached, and neither source is named.

18:8.note: 'As ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another's burdens, that they may be light.' The most famous sentence in the Book of Mormon's covenant, and it is Galatians 6:2 with the second-person pronoun removed. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is not one of his thirty-six; it is catalogued as a quotation here on CONVENTIONS §2's grounds — a complete clause reproduced from a verse that is identifiably and uniquely its source. Note the 1830 reading 'here is the waters of Mormon', corrected to 'are' in 1920: the first edition's grammar is the looser one throughout this chapter.
18:8.text: Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

provenance.other: 'Fold' stands in 49 KJV verses, most of them the verb; “one fold” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:16. The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'the fold of God', which is in no KJV verse at all, so the contact is with the image and not with a string.
provenance.alternative: The pastoral image is common property — Psalm 100:3, Ezekiel 34, John 10 — and 'fold of God' may simply be the natural English for a flock that belongs to God.
provenance.significance: If John 10:16 is in view it is worth knowing what comes with it: the verse is Jesus promising 'other sheep I have, which are not of this fold ... and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd', which is the single New Testament sentence the Book of Mormon most insists is about itself (3 Nephi 15–16 makes it the hinge of the whole visitation). Alma inviting a hidden congregation in the wilderness to 'come into the fold of God' would then be the book's first, unannounced use of the verse it will later claim outright.

18:8.note: Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a rather than argued: the wording will not carry an allusion, but the phrase sits in a book that later stakes a great deal on this one verse, and a reader who knows 3 Nephi 15:21 will hear it here.
18:8.whyNot: No shared string longer than the word 'fold', and the sheepfold is the common stock of biblical pastoral language. If this is a borrowing it is unprovable from the wording alone.
18:8.text: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.

provenance.route: Romans 12:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Isaiah 61:2's verb substituted
provenance.other: Three rarities converge. “weep with them that weep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 12:15, which supplies the whole construction — a verb of grief, 'with', and the same verb again as a participle for its objects. “comfort all that mourn” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 61:2, which supplies the substituted verb; and “comfort them which” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 1:4, whose object is 'them which are in any trouble'.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Romans 12:15's construction is reproduced exactly and its verb is replaced by Isaiah 61:2's, so that 'mourn with those that mourn' says in Paul's grammar what Isaiah's servant was anointed to do. Isaiah 61 is the passage Jesus reads in the synagogue at Nazareth and claims for himself (Luke 4:18–19), and Luke's citation stops one clause short of 'to comfort all that mourn'. Alma, founding a church in hiding, writes the unread clause into the entrance requirement: what the Book of Mormon's covenant asks of every member is the office Isaiah assigns to the anointed one.

18:9.note: 'Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort.' Romans 12:15's construction with Isaiah 61:2's verb, followed by a comfort clause built on the figura etymologica of 2 Corinthians 1:4 — comforting the comfortless with the comfort received. All three sources are exhortations to a congregation about its internal life, which is exactly the office the sentence is performing.
18:9.text: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.

provenance.other: “the first resurrection” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 20:5 and 20:6, and nowhere else in the Bible. Both are within four verses of each other in the millennium vision; there is no Old Testament source for the phrase.
provenance.significance: Revelation 20:6 says three things about those who have part in the first resurrection: the second death has no power on them, they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and they shall reign with him. Alma's covenant promises the first — 'that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection' — and then, within nine verses, performs the second: at 18:18 he 'ordained priests, even one priest to every fifty of their number'. The apocalypse's promise of a priesthood for the first-resurrection company is realised in the chapter's own narrative as an ordination at the waters of Mormon.

18:9.note: 'That ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life.' A phrase with exactly one home in the KJV, and it is the Apocalypse, six hundred years and one testament away from the speaker. Also worth naming: 'stand as witnesses of God at all times, and in all things, and in all places', which has no KJV phrase behind it but occupies Acts 1:8's office ('ye shall be witnesses unto me ... unto the uttermost part of the earth') and is recorded here rather than given a link of its own.
18:9.text: Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years.

provenance.other: “what doth hinder me to be baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:36. It is the Bible's only sentence in which the question of an impediment to baptism is put in so many words, and it is put by the candidate. Alma's 'what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord' asks the same question from the other side of the water, in modern English rather than the KJV's. Frederick's co-occurrence index (data/frederick-refs.json) records Mosiah 18:10 discussed within 1500 characters of Acts 2:38 and Acts 8:16 in Frederick 2016; that index measures adjacency on a page, not a proposed source, and his book — which argues about the Gospel of John — has no cross-reference apparatus. It is noted here as a bookmark and is not evidence for this link.
provenance.alternative: Acts 10:47, 'Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized', asks the impediment question from the officiant's side, which is Alma's side; but it shares no wording at all with Mosiah 18:10, where Acts 8:36 shares the construction.
provenance.significance: The eunuch's question is asked at a roadside water in the middle of nowhere, by a man reading a prophet he does not understand, and answered by a confession of faith; Alma's is asked at a hidden fountain by a fugitive who has just been expounding a prophet his hearers did not understand, and answered by a covenant. The Book of Mormon has kept the setting of Acts 8 — the unlikely water, the private catechesis, the immediate baptism — and replaced the eunuch's christological confession with a covenant to 'serve him and keep his commandments', which is the substitution the whole chapter is organised around.

18:10.note: 'Now I say unto you, if this be the desires of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord.' The KJV's one impediment-to-baptism question, turned round from candidate to officiant and de-archaised. Catalogued at moderate confidence because the modernised wording is exactly what makes the case arguable rather than demonstrable: the construction is Acts 8:36's, the diction is not. The 1830 plural 'desires of your hearts', singular in 1920 and again at 18:11, is the first edition's reading in both verses.
18:10.text: And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?

provenance.route: Joel 2:28 or Acts 2:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the verse cannot decide between them
provenance.other: “pour out my spirit” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Proverbs 1:23 and Joel 2:28 and 2:29; Acts 2:17, quoting Joel, reads 'I will pour out of my Spirit' with the partitive 'of'. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence at this verse, and the reason is instructive: the Book of Mormon has 'pour out his spirit', third person, because Alma is speaking about God rather than as God, so the pronoun that would carry the test is not there and the partitive 'of' has nothing to attach to.
provenance.alternative: 'Pour out' with 'spirit' is also Ezekiel 39:29, Zechariah 12:10 and Proverbs 1:23; no one verse is required.
provenance.significance: The phrase governs three consecutive verses of the chapter — the promise at 18:10, Alma's prayer at 18:12 ('O Lord, pour out thy spirit upon thy servant'), and the baptismal formula at 18:13 ('may the spirit of the Lord be poured out upon you') — and it is the language of Pentecost in both Testaments. Whichever form stands behind it, Alma is describing the founding of a church in the words of the founding of the Church.

18:10.note: Recorded chiefly for the mediation result, which is negative and worth having: this is a case where an Old Testament verse and its New Testament quotation differ at exactly one word and the Book of Mormon's grammar removes the word. The test cannot be run here, and `mediation` is 'uncertain' as CONVENTIONS §7 requires rather than defaulted to either side.
18:10.whyNot: 'Pour out' plus 'spirit' is one of the commonest prophetic collocations in the KJV and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly; nothing in this verse points at Joel in particular.
18:10.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

provenance.other: “buried with him” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 6:4 and Colossians 2:12, which are the Bible's only two statements that baptism is a burial. They differ in what follows: Romans 6:4 moves from the burial to the believer walking 'in newness of life' — “newness of life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — while Colossians 2:12 has the believer rise, 'wherein also ye are risen with him'. Mosiah 18:14 has the rising: 'both Alma and Helam was buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing'. tools/mediation-check.py finds one decisive point for Colossians, but a weak one; the argument here rests on the rising, which is a clause the tool's word-level comparison cannot see.
provenance.significance: Paul's burial metaphor is a figure of speech about what baptism means; the Book of Mormon literalises it. Alma does not say that Helam was buried with Christ, he says both men 'was buried in the water' and then 'arose and came forth out of the water' — so the burial and the resurrection are things that physically happen to two bodies in a pond, and the second man baptised in the new church is baptised by immersion because Colossians says so. Note the consequence at 18:15: Alma, having been buried alongside Helam, 'did not bury himself again in the water', which is a piece of practical reasoning about a metaphor.

18:14.note: 'And after Alma had said these words, both Alma and Helam was buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing, being filled with the spirit.' The 1830 reading 'was buried' — a singular verb under the compound subject, corrected to 'were' in 1920 — is the first edition's, and it matters slightly: the singular reads the two men as one act, which is what makes 18:15's exemption intelligible. The verse is the clearest place in the Book of Mormon where a Pauline figure has been turned back into a rubric.
18:14.text: Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead.

provenance.other: “the same day there were added” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:41, and “they that gladly received his word” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Acts 2:41 is the only verse in the Bible that counts converts at a mass baptism with the formula 'about [number] souls'; Mosiah 18:16 counts them as 'about two hundred and four souls'.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's church is founded with Pentecost's census formula and one seventh-part of Pentecost's number, at a pond in the wilderness rather than in Jerusalem before three thousand. Recovering Acts 2:41's context makes the resemblance denser than the count: 'they that gladly received his word were baptized' matches Mosiah 18:6–7's 'as many as believed him, went thither to hear his words' almost step for step, and the sequence hearing → belief → mass baptism → counted souls is Luke's order exactly. The oddity is the number itself. 204 is not a round figure and not a biblical one; a writer imitating Acts 2:41 would have no reason to invent it, which is one of the better arguments in the chapter that the imitation is not merely decorative.

18:16.note: 'They were in number about two hundred and four souls; yea, and they were baptized in the waters of Mormon, and were filled with the grace of God.' The 'about ... souls' construction is Acts 2:41's and no one else's in the KJV. This link and the one at 18:17 are two halves of a single borrowing — Luke reports the founding congregation's number in verse 41 and its increase in verse 47, and Mosiah 18 reports them in verses 16 and 17.
18:16.text: Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.

provenance.other: “added to the church” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:47: 'And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.' It is the New Testament's founding sentence about how a church grows, and the Book of Mormon reproduces four of its words with the possessive changed: 'whosoever was baptized by the power and authority of God, they was added to his church.'
provenance.significance: Luke's grammar makes the Lord the subject — the Lord adds, the church receives — and Alma's sentence keeps that and adds a condition Luke does not state: 'by the power and authority of God'. So the verse simultaneously borrows the New Testament's charter of church growth and inserts into it the doctrine of authority that the Book of Mormon, and the movement that published it, needed the charter to contain. That insertion is the interesting half. Acts 2:47 says nothing about who may baptise; Mosiah 18:17 makes the addition contingent on it, and 18:13's 'having authority from the Almighty God' has already supplied the formula.

18:17.note: 'And they were called the Church of God, or the Church of Christ, from that time forward. And it came to pass that whosoever was baptized by the power and authority of God, they was added to his church.' A four-word KJV singleton carrying Acts 2's whole ecclesiology, and the 1830 reading is the more visibly borrowed one: 'they was added to his church', where 1920 deletes the redundant pronoun. The first edition's syntax is Luke's clause with a resumptive subject bolted on, which is what a writer working from a remembered KJV sentence produces and what a careful editor removes.
18:17.text: Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.

18:18.text: To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:

provenance.other: “things pertaining to the kingdom of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:3, and Mosiah 18:18 reproduces all eight words in order, with 'concerning the' where Luke has 'speaking of'. The shorter “pertaining to the kingdom” is a singleton in the same verse. The organisational detail beside it — 'one priest to every fifty of their number' — has no KJV phrase behind it, though fifty as the unit under one appointed man is the Pentateuch's ('rulers of fifties', Exodus 18:21).
provenance.significance: Acts 1:3 is a summary of syllabus: it describes what the risen Christ taught the apostles during the forty days between the resurrection and the ascension, and it is the only place the KJV names that curriculum. Alma ordains priests and gives them the same syllabus verbatim. Read with 18:2 — where Alma's own preaching is summarised as 'the resurrection of the dead, and the redemption of the people ... and his resurrection and ascension into Heaven', which is Acts 1's subject matter in Acts 1's order — the chapter is founding a church on the forty days' instruction, and then, at 18:16–17, populating it with Acts 2's Pentecost census. The Book of Mormon's first church is built through the first two chapters of Acts in sequence.

18:18.note: 'Alma, having authority from God, ordained priests; even one priest to every fifty of their number did he ordain to preach unto them, and to teach them concerning the things pertaining to the kingdom of God.' An eight-word verbatim run from a KJV singleton, which is the longest exact borrowing in the chapter and the one the n-gram stream ranked highest (3.51). It sits below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six; it is catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the clause is complete, exact, and has one possible source.

provenance.other: Three Pauline unity texts, each identified by a rarity. “one faith one baptism” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:5. “knit together in” is a KJV singleton, Colossians 2:2 — 'that their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love'; 2:19 reads 'knit together, increaseth', a different construction with no 'in' at all, not a second instance. “no divisions among you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 1:10, whose subject is contention in a congregation.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 4:4–6 is a seven-fold litany — one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God — and Alma takes exactly the two items that a newly baptised congregation could be said to hold in common, drops the rest, and prefixes his own: 'they should look forward with one eye'. That phrase is in no KJV verse. So the verse is a Pauline formula with a non-Pauline first term inserted at the head of it, and the inserted term is the one that turns a creed into a discipline — Ephesians lists what the church already shares, Alma commands what it must do.

18:21.note: 'And he commanded them that there should be no contention one with another, but that they should look forward with one eye, having one faith and one baptism; having their hearts knit together in unity and in love, one towards another.' Three of Paul's four great appeals against congregational division, fused into a single sentence in the order 1 Corinthians → Ephesians → Colossians: no divisions, one faith and one baptism, hearts knit together in love. Each is identifiable by an absolute or near-absolute rarity, and none is named.
18:21.text: One Lord, one faith, one baptism,

provenance.route: Exodus 20:8 + Exodus 31:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: A composite of two singletons. “keep it holy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 20:8, the fourth commandment in its Exodus form; “observe the sabbath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 31:16. Run against the Deuteronomic form of the commandment, tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Exodus 20:8 — the Book of Mormon has Exodus's 'keep' where Deuteronomy 5:12 has 'sanctify', and Exodus's 'holy' where Deuteronomy has 'as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee'. Its third reported point, that the Book of Mormon has Deuteronomy's 'Keep' rather than Exodus's 'Remember', is an artifact of the tool matching the 'keep' of 'keep it holy'; the Book of Mormon's actual leading verb is 'observe', which is neither, and which is Exodus 31:16's.
provenance.significance: Exodus 31:16 is not a repetition of the commandment but its covenant clause: Israel keeps the sabbath 'throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant', and it is a sign between God and Israel for ever. Mosiah 18 is a covenant chapter — the word governs 18:10 and 18:13 — and the one sabbath verse in the KJV that makes the sabbath itself a perpetual covenant is the one supplying Alma's verb. So the sabbath command given to the new church at Mormon is worded out of the two Exodus verses that between them make sabbath-keeping the sign of the covenant rather than merely a law within it.

18:23.note: 'And he commanded them that they should observe the sabbath day, and keep it holy, and also every day they should give thanks to the Lord their God.' Two Exodus singletons welded, and the Deuteronomic form of the commandment demonstrably not in view. The second clause quietly undoes the first — a people commanded to keep one day holy and then to give thanks 'every day' — which is the same move the New Testament makes on the sabbath and which the Book of Mormon makes here without argument.
18:23.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

provenance.other: “with our own hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 27:19 (jettisoning a ship's tackle) and 1 Corinthians 4:12, 'And labour, working with our own hands'. Only the second is about a minister's self-support, and it is the New Testament's programmatic statement of it. 2 Thessalonians 3:8 supplies the negative half that Mosiah 18:26 states — 'that we might not be chargeable to any of you'.
provenance.significance: Paul's tentmaking is an argument, not a biography: he works with his own hands so that the gospel shall be 'without charge' and no one may say he preached for money. Alma legislates it, which no New Testament writer does — 1 Corinthians 9 in fact defends the opposite right at length — and legislates it immediately after ordaining priests, in a chapter whose villains are the priests of Noah, a paid clergy supported by a fifth of the people's substance (Mosiah 11:3). The borrowing is therefore polemical: the anti-priestcraft rule of the new church is written in the words of the apostle who declined to be paid, and it is aimed at the priesthood the reader has just watched burn a prophet.

18:24.note: 'And he also commanded them that the priests which he had ordained should labor with their own hands for their support.' The phrase is Paul's and the setting supplies the argument the phrase carries; what the Book of Mormon adds is the commandment, since Paul offers his practice as a personal renunciation of a right rather than a rule for others. The 1830 'the priests which he had ordained', modernized to 'whom' in 1920, is the KJV's own relative-pronoun usage.
18:24.whyNot: Working with one's hands is common enough in the KJV (Ephesians 4:28, 1 Thessalonians 4:11) that no single verse is required, and 'labor for their support' is not KJV diction at all.
18:24.text: And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:

provenance.other: “according to that a man hath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 8:12, and the whole of its construction is reproduced: Paul's 'accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not' becomes 'according to that which he hath ... and to him that hath not should be given'. The final clause inverts a second singleton: “hath not shall be taken” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:29, 'but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath'. Acts 4:35's 'distribution was made unto every man according as he had need' stands behind 18:29's 'according to their needs and their wants'.
provenance.significance: The inversion at the end of the verse is the finding. Matthew's parable of the talents states the harshest economic sentence in the gospels — to him that hath, more; from him that hath not, even what he has — and Alma's rule ends 'and to him that hath not should be given'. The Book of Mormon takes the KJV's one occurrence of that clause and reverses its verb, so that the law of the church at Mormon is the parable of the talents run backwards. Paul's collection principle supplies the first half of the sentence and the Matthean reversal supplies the last four words, and the two together are a redistribution rule assembled out of two passages neither of which is one.

18:27.note: 'Every one according to that which he hath; if he have more abundantly, he should impart more abundantly; and he that hath but little, but little should be required; and to him that hath not should be given.' Paul's Jerusalem-collection formula, with the graduated middle clauses of 2 Corinthians 8:13–14 compressed and the tail turned against Matthew 25:29. The verse carries five 1830 variants, all of them the first edition's looser grammar ('according to that which he hath' for 1920's 'had'), and the present-tense 'hath' is the KJV's own tense in 2 Corinthians 8:12 — the 1920 correction to 'had' moves the sentence away from its source.
18:27.text: For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.

provenance.other: 'Of their own free will' is in no KJV verse in that form; the nearest is Ezra 7:13's 'of their own freewill' (of pilgrims volunteering for Jerusalem) and the freewill offerings of Leviticus 22 and Deuteronomy 16. 2 Corinthians 9:7's contribution is the doctrine rather than the string: 'not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver'.
provenance.significance: The two verses of Mosiah 18:27–28 run the two chapters of Paul's collection appeal in order — 2 Corinthians 8 supplies the proportional rule, 2 Corinthians 9 the requirement that the giving be voluntary — and the second is the one that makes the first bearable. Alma has just imposed a graduated levy; the next sentence makes it a free will offering, which is precisely the move 2 Corinthians 9:7 makes after 8:12–14.

18:28.note: 'And thus they should impart of their substance, of their own free will and good desires towards God, and to those priests that stood in need, yea, and to every needy, naked soul.' Recorded as an echo because the phrase is the Old Testament's freewill-offering language rather than Paul's wording, but the sequence is 2 Corinthians 8 then 9, in Paul's order, and it follows a verse that is demonstrably 2 Corinthians 8:12. The closing 'every needy, naked soul' reaches instead for the prophetic almsgiving formula of Isaiah 58:7, 'when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him'.
18:28.whyNot: Not one distinctive string is shared with 2 Corinthians 9:7; the case is entirely that 18:27 is demonstrably from the previous chapter of the same appeal and this sentence does the next thing that appeal does.
18:28.text: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

provenance.other: “how beautiful” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Song of Solomon 7:1, Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15. Within the Book of Mormon the phrase has already been used five times in six chapters, all of them Abinadi's: Mosiah 12:21 quotes Isaiah 52:7 entire, and Mosiah 15:15, 15:16, 15:17 and 15:18 expound it a clause at a time. Every one of those five reads 'how beautiful upon the mountains'. Mosiah 18:30 drops the mountains and pluralises the subject — 'how beautiful are they' — and those are precisely the two ways Romans 10:15 departs from Isaiah 52:7 ('How beautiful are the feet of them'). tools/mediation-check.py, run on Isaiah 52:7 against Romans 10:15, reports one decisive point each way and calls the verse a composite.
provenance.alternative: The mountains and the feet may have gone for the plainest of reasons: Alma's subject is not a messenger but a place — the forest, the fountain, the waters — and 'how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet' cannot be said of a pond. On that reading the plural and the missing mountains are grammar, not Romans, and the verse is straightforwardly Isaiah reached through Abinadi.
provenance.significance: The route is the finding, and it is the clearest instance so far of a source arriving in the Book of Mormon by way of an earlier Book of Mormon quotation rather than the Bible. Alma heard Isaiah 52:7 from Abinadi — 17:4 says he 'did write all the words which Abinadi had spoken' — and 18:30 is the sentence in which he applies it, not to a herald on a mountain but to the place where he baptised. Recovering the source's context does the rest: Isaiah 52:7's good tidings are that the exile is over and 'Thy God reigneth', and Alma is a fugitive in a forest hiding from a king. The next verses prove the point: 18:31, 'that they might not come to the knowledge of the king'; 18:34, the flight into the wilderness. The verse that publishes peace is spoken by people who are about to run.

18:30.note: 'The place of Mormon, the waters of Mormon, the forest of Mormon, how beautiful are they to the eyes of them who there came to the knowledge of their redeemer.' Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 52:7 here and the link is not in doubt; what the catalogue adds is the route and the departure. Abinadi's five uses of the verse in Mosiah 12 and 15 all keep 'upon the mountains'; Alma's drops it, and drops it in the direction of the New Testament's citation of the same verse. Whether that is Romans or simply the demands of the sentence is set out in the alternative above and is not settled here.
18:30.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “stirreth up the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 23:5, where it is the charge the accusers press on Pilate after his first attempt to dismiss the case. “mover of sedition” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 24:5, Tertullus's parallel charge against Paul before Felix. The Book of Mormon's 'stirring up the people to a rebellion against him' has the first verb and the second's political content.
provenance.significance: This closes a circuit begun in the previous chapter. Mosiah 17:12's 'began to accuse him, saying' is Luke 23:2, the accusation laid before Pilate; Mosiah 18:33's 'stirring up the people' is Luke 23:5, the accusation renewed three verses later when Pilate tries to let the prisoner go. The Book of Mormon has taken two consecutive charges from one hearing and distributed them across two generations of the same conflict — the first kills Abinadi, the second sends Alma into the wilderness — and it takes them in Luke's order. That is a stronger argument for the chapter-17 links than anything inside chapter 17.

18:33.note: 'And now the king saith that Alma was stirring up the people to a rebellion against him; therefore he sent his army to destroy them.' A KJV singleton, and the second half of a two-part borrowing from the same Lukan hearing that supplied Mosiah 17:12. The 1830 present tense 'the king saith', modernised to 'said' in 1920, is worth noting: the first edition reports the charge in the tense the KJV uses for accusations in progress.
18:33.text: And they were the more fierce, saying, He stirreth up the people, teaching throughout all Jewry, beginning from Galilee to this place.
